title: Rose's civil rights activism; separating art from the social
summary: Rose says Russell's approach is more social than his. He has been jailed for rent strikes and civil rights work but keeps that apart from the music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Well, I wonder, you mentioned that, uh, that Bill doesn't think it, Bill Russell doesn't think it that important.
Russell is much concerned with, for instance, the plight of the, of the black, not necessarily even the musicians. Mm-hmm. Um, I'm concerned, too, about the plight of the black and always have been.

I'm not only concerned, but I have been actively involved in the, in, uh, in the struggles of the black. I mean, I have been in jail for my participation in the struggles of the black and in the organization of rent strikes and other phenomena like that.

But this is not to say that, uh, that I necessarily, uh, carry that through and confuse it, as I think of it, with the nature of the music, which is an entirely separate matter. And, uh, uh, uh, so, so that Russell's, uh, uh, attitude about it is much more a social attitude than mine.
I wonder, I wonder, Al, whether, whether you can really separate the artistic from the social and political, uh...

Oh, yes, because, uh, it is necessary to understand a society and a social context before you can get a full appreciation and understanding the music. But it is not necessary to understand the musician. It is not necessary to know anything about him, because if your ear can't tell you what the message is, it doesn't make any difference who the man is. Mm-hmm. So that, uh, uh, it, it has never mattered to me who's playing a...
